name: Ichiran
editorialNote: Best known for its individual counter booths, designed to remove distraction and let a diner focus entirely on the bowl -- a genuinely original piece of ramen-shop design that's since become one of Hakata tonkotsu's most recognized global ambassadors.
sourceNotes: Widely documented chain origin story (individual booth seating); official website confirmed.

name: Ippudo
editorialNote: One of the shops most credited with taking Hakata-style tonkotsu international, opening its first overseas location in the 2000s and helping introduce the style to diners well outside Japan.
sourceNotes: Widely documented international expansion history; official website confirmed.

name: Nankin Senryo
editorialNote: Credited in ramen histories as the 1937 origin point of the emulsified, hard-boiled tonkotsu technique -- the method later refined and popularized a short distance away in Hakata.
sourceNotes: Widely repeated origin attribution in ramen histories (1937, Kurume); current official website not confidently verified, so omitted rather than guessed.

name: Taishoken
editorialNote: Founded by Kazuo Yamagishi in Higashi-Ikebukuro in 1961, and widely called the origin shop of tsukemen -- the separated noodle-and-dipping-broth format documented on this app's Tsukemen entry.
sourceNotes: Widely documented 1961 origin attribution (Kazuo Yamagishi); current official website not confidently verified, so omitted rather than guessed.

name: Yoshimuraya
editorialNote: Founded by Yoshimura Minoru in 1974, and the shop the entire Iekei ("house-style") lineage traces back to -- the tonkotsu-shoyu hybrid documented on this app's Yokohama Iekei entry.
sourceNotes: Widely documented 1974 origin attribution (Yoshimura Minoru); current official website not confidently verified, so omitted rather than guessed.

name: Menya Hanabi
editorialNote: Invented "Taiwan mazesoba" in 2008, the brothless tossed-noodle dish that spread nationwide from this single Nagoya shop within about a decade.
sourceNotes: Widely documented 2008 origin attribution; current official website not confidently verified, so omitted rather than guessed.

name: Misen
editorialNote: Created Nagoya Taiwan Ramen in the 1970s under Taiwanese-born chef Kaku Gakusei -- the fiery, garlic-and-chili noodle soup named for the chef's origin, not the dish's.
sourceNotes: Widely documented 1970s origin attribution (Kaku Gakusei); current official website not confidently verified, so omitted rather than guessed.

name: Aji no Sanpei
editorialNote: Widely credited with pairing miso tare with ramen for the first time in the mid-1950s, making it the origin point of the style that became Sapporo's signature.
sourceNotes: Widely repeated origin attribution in ramen histories (mid-1950s); current official website not confidently verified, so omitted rather than guessed.

name: Miyoshi
editorialNote: Credited with originating abura soba in Musashino in the 1950s -- the brothless, tossed-noodle dish that predates and developed independently of Nagoya's later, unrelated mazesoba.
sourceNotes: Widely repeated origin attribution (1950s, Musashino); current official website not confidently verified, so omitted rather than guessed.
